lists.title: Pre-flight — before ANY playbook touches production
lists.intro: Run this every time, even when you're sure. Especially when you're sure. Aviation runs checklists precisely because the pilots are experts, not despite it.

items.text: ansible-playbook <play> --syntax-check
items.why: Catches YAML and structure errors in seconds. The cheapest gate there is.

items.text: ansible-playbook <play> --list-hosts
items.why: Confirms the blast radius. Read every hostname. If the list surprises you, STOP.

items.text: ansible-playbook <play> --check --diff --limit <one-host>
items.why: Dry-run on one victim. Read the diff like you'll be quizzed on it. Remember command/shell tasks don't honor check mode.

items.text: Run for real with --limit <one-host>, then VERIFY on that host by hand
items.why: One host proves the change; the recap alone proves nothing. stat the file, curl the service, whatever 'working' means here.

items.text: Now the fleet — and watch the recap for unreachable= and failed=
items.why: Non-zero unreachable on a normal day means inventory drift — chase it today, not someday.

items.text: Log what you ran and the recap counts in the ops log / scar ledger
items.why: Future-you, three weeks from now, will need to know what changed today.

lists.title: Friday close-out ritual
lists.intro: Twenty minutes on Friday buys a calm Monday. Do not skip the commit.

items.text: git status in the playbook repo — commit or stash everything, push to origin
items.why: Uncommitted Friday work is Monday's mystery. The repo is the source of truth only if the truth is in it.

items.text: ansible all -m ping > /tmp/census-$(date +%F).txt — save the fleet census
items.why: A dated reachability snapshot. When something's down Monday, you'll know if it died over the weekend or before.

items.text: systemctl list-units --failed on the control node
items.why: Leave your own house clean. A sick control node poisons every diagnosis.

items.text: df -h on the control node — anything above 80%?
items.why: Disks fill on weekends when nobody's watching. 80% Friday is 100% Sunday night.

items.text: Write tomorrow-you one line: what's half-done and where you left it
items.why: The context you dump now is the context Monday-you won't have to rebuild.

lists.title: PANIC — something is wrong and I don't know what
lists.intro: Stop typing. Breathe. You are not the first person here, and this page has your back. Do these in order — no skipping ahead to fixes.

items.text: STOP the bleeding: if a playbook is mid-run and wrecking things, Ctrl-C it. That aborts the run immediately — but tasks already launched on targets will finish on their own.
items.why: A stopped bad run is recoverable. Note which hosts had already started before you killed it — those are your blast radius.

items.text: Do NOT 'fix' anything yet. Write down (paper is fine): what you ran, when, what you expected, what you saw.
items.why: The first fix attempted in panic usually destroys the evidence and often makes it worse.

items.text: Establish blast radius: which hosts did it touch? Scroll the recap or the log, and preview the same command's targets:
items.why: One host wrong is an incident. Fifty hosts wrong is a different procedure — know which you're in.

items.text: Check the fleet's pulse:
items.why: Facts beat fear. Often the damage is smaller than the adrenaline says.
items.cmd:
ansible all -m ping
ansible <affected-group> -m command -a 'systemctl list-units --failed' 2>/dev/null

items.text: Read the actual error — paste it into the Error Decoder and read the matched explanation fully before acting.
items.why: The decoder maps symptoms to diseases. Treating the disease beats treating the symptom.

items.text: If data may be lost or a system is compromised: hands off, escalate per the dossier's contact list. That is strength, not weakness.
items.why: Recovery and forensics both degrade with every keystroke on the patient. Knowing when to stop IS the senior skill.

items.text: Afterward — same day — write the scar ledger entry.
items.why: The ledger is how this seat gets safer every year. Pay it forward.

lists.title: Day One recon — know your terrain before touching anything
lists.intro: Run these read-only commands on the control node your first day (and on any unfamiliar box, forever). Each one draws part of the map. Nothing here changes state.

items.expect: Version, and 'config file =' pointing at the config you expect.
items.ifnot: A None or surprising config file means settings come from somewhere you haven't found yet. Chase it before anything else — precedence: $ANSIBLE_CONFIG, ./ansible.cfg, ~/.ansible.cfg, /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg.

items.expect: A short list of deliberate-looking overrides, each naming its origin file.
items.ifnot: Settings you can't explain = archaeology required. Each one was someone's scar; find the story before you 'clean it up'.

items.expect: A group tree that matches what you were told this estate looks like.
items.ifnot: Empty or weird tree: wrong inventory path in config, or the inventory lives somewhere else. ansible-config dump | grep -i inventory.

items.expect: Either an error ('Could not match') — good, implicit localhost — or vars including ansible_connection: local.
items.ifnot: localhost defined WITHOUT ansible_connection=local means delegation will SSH to your own control node and hang. Scar #001. Fix before your first playbook run.

items.expect: SUCCESS/pong from every host (or a known, documented list of exceptions).
items.ifnot: Every failure is either inventory drift or a dead host. Triage each with the UNREACHABLE tree; update the dossier.

items.expect: The repo/config directory NOT world-writable; ansible.cfg a real file (or a symlink you can explain).
items.ifnot: World-writable directory = Ansible silently ignores ./ansible.cfg. Symlinks: know which end is the real file — git versions what the repo path holds.
A dirty tree or stale history means the repo may NOT be the real source of truth yet. Find out what is before editing anything.
A sick control node lies to you in a hundred small ways. Heal the doctor first.
Unknown logins on the automation controller are a security question — ask it today.

items.expect: You can explain every scheduled job and timer, or the dossier can.
items.ifnot: Unknown scheduled jobs are landmines with timers. Read each script it calls; paste any known CLI commands inside them into the Command Decoder (the decoder can't explain arbitrary scripts — read those yourself). Write findings into the dossier.

items.expect: System clock synchronised to a source; offset well under a second.
items.ifnot: Clock drift on an air-gapped enclave breaks Kerberos/TLS/2FA and makes cross-host log timelines lie. Find the enclave's time source (dossier) and fix chrony.conf before trusting any log forensics.

lists.title: The Forbidden List
lists.intro: Rules with scars behind them. Break one knowingly and you'd better be able to explain why to the next person who sits here.

items.rule: Never run ansible all -m shell (or command) with a state-changing command and no --limit.
items.story: One typo'd sed against 'all' rewrites a config on every machine you own in under a minute. The fleet-wide fix took a weekend; the --limit would have taken four seconds.
A new admin 'added' a user to one group and silently removed them from six, including the one that granted sudo. Lockout, on a Friday, naturally. -aG or nothing.

items.rule: Never edit sudoers with anything but visudo (or drop-ins validated by visudo -c).
items.story: One missing colon in sudoers disables sudo for every human on the box. With root login disabled too, that's a console walk — or a rescue boot.
It 'fixed' the app in thirty seconds and failed the audit in thirty days — and the relabel on re-enable took the service down for hours. The real fix was one restorecon.

items.rule: Never rm from a find you haven't run bare first.
items.story: find with a subtly wrong -mtime deleted current logs instead of old ones. The bare run would have shown the mistake in the first ten lines of output.

items.rule: Never kill -9 as the first resort, and never on databases.
items.story: SIGKILL'd database, corrupted WAL, restore from backup — four hours. systemctl stop would have taken ninety seconds.

items.rule: Never reboot a box you can't console into, without knowing WHY it's sick.
items.story: The reboot 'fixed' it right up until the box didn't come back — the disk was dying, and the reboot was the coup de grâce. Uptime was the only thing keeping the evidence alive.

items.rule: Never put secrets in playbooks, inventory, or logs in plaintext. Vault or nothing.
items.story: A password in group_vars went to the git remote; the remote got mirrored; the mirror got shared. Rotation, apology tour, new rule. ansible-vault exists precisely for this.

items.rule: Never run a playbook you haven't read against hosts that matter.
items.story: A downloaded 'hardening' playbook helpfully disabled password AND key auth. Read every task; --list-tasks is the two-second X-ray.

lists.title: New host enrollment — from cabled to fleet member
lists.intro: The ladder for bringing a fresh RHEL box under Ansible control. Every rung exists elsewhere in this kit; this is the order.

items.text: Verify the host's SSH fingerprint out-of-band (console), then enroll it: ssh-keyscan <host> >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
items.why: Pre-populating known_hosts is what lets batch runs never hang on a host-key prompt — without blanket-disabling checking.

items.text: Create the automation user on the host (console or -k first contact): useradd + wheel/sudoers policy per the dossier's auth model
items.why: Automation should never run as your personal account — attribution and revocation both need a dedicated user.

items.text: Install the automation key: ssh-copy-id -i <key.pub> <user>@<host> (or the authorized_key snippet once Ansible can reach it)
items.why: Key auth is what makes the fleet drivable without invisible password prompts.

items.text: sudoers drop-in for the automation user (NOPASSWD or vaulted become per site policy) — validate with visudo -c
items.why: become without a password plan = the silent-hang scar. Decide the policy now, on purpose.

items.text: Add the host to inventory in its right group; commit the inventory change to git
items.why: The repo is the source of truth — a host that exists only in your terminal history doesn't exist.

items.text: Prove the whole ladder: ansible <host> -m ping, then ansible <host> -m setup -a 'filter=ansible_distribution*'
items.why: pong proves transport AND Python module execution; facts prove the box is fully conversational.

items.text: Record the host and any quirks in the Estate Dossier
items.why: Day-one you wished someone had done this. Be the someone.

lists.title: 30 / 60 / 90 — from surviving to owning the seat
lists.intro: Check items off as you demonstrate them (progress saves in this browser). Done doesn't mean 'read about it' — it means 'did it on a real or lab box'.

items.text: Complete Day One recon on the control node; every finding written into the Estate Dossier
Run the full pre-flight ritual on a real change, --limit one host, verified by hand
Read every play in the repo top to bottom; decode anything cryptic with the Command Decoder
Drill: diagnose the hanging-playbook scenario without looking at the answer
Read scar ledger entries #001 and #002 and explain both diseases out loud to someone (or a rubber duck)
Author a new playbook with the Task Builder; ship it through the full pre-flight ritual
Handle one real failure using the decision trees; add anything new to the scar ledger
Rekey or verify ansible-vault handling; prove you can rotate the vault password safely
Drill: the disk-full and service-down scenarios, cold
Explain runtime-vs-permanent in firewalld and enable-vs-start in systemd without notes
Complete an OS patch cycle (dnf) on a host group with rollback plan and verification
Add one new decision tree or five new command entries from your own experience — export annotations and merge them
Run a restore test: prove one backup actually restores. Backups that were never restored are rumors
Teach one thing from this kit to someone else. Teaching is the exit exam
Write your own letter paragraph for the next person. You're the greybeard now — start acting like it
